title: LINQ Basics
description: Use Language Integrated Query (LINQ) to filter, sort, group, and transform data in C# collections.

data.text: LINQ (Language Integrated Query) brings the power of database-style queries directly into C#. Instead of writing manual loops, conditionals, and sorting logic, you express what you want in a declarative way. LINQ works on any data source that implements IEnumerable<T> — arrays, lists, databases, XML, and even custom types.

LINQ offers two equivalent syntax styles. Method syntax uses chainable extension methods like Where, Select, and OrderBy. Query syntax uses SQL-like keywords (from, where, select) that the compiler translates into method calls. Both produce the same result — choose the one that reads better for the problem at hand.

data.title: Method Syntax vs. Query Syntax
data.content: Same logic written in both LINQ styles

data.text: LINQ provides dozens of operators. The most frequently used ones fall into a handful of categories: filtering (Where), transformation (Select), sorting (OrderBy, OrderByDescending), aggregation (Sum, Average, Count, Max, Min), and element access (First, Last, Single). Each returns an IEnumerable<T> (except aggregators, which return a scalar), making them composable in long chains.

data.content: Demonstrates Where, Select, OrderBy, Count, Sum, Any, All, First, and Distinct

data.text: GroupBy organizes elements into buckets based on a key, returning an IEnumerable<IGrouping<TKey, TElement>>. Each IGrouping acts like a sub-list for one key. Join connects two sequences based on matching keys, similar to an SQL INNER JOIN, using a key selector for each side.

data.text: Most LINQ operators use deferred execution: the query is not run when you build it, but when you iterate the result (e.g., with foreach, ToList(), ToArray()). This means the source is re-enumerated on each iteration, and changes to the source after query construction are reflected in the results. Operators like ToList(), ToArray(), Count(), and First() force immediate execution.

data.title: Deferred Execution in Action
data.content: Demonstrates that the query runs only when iterated

data.title: Deferred Execution Gotcha
data.text: If your source collection changes between building the query and iterating it, the results will change too. Call ToList() or ToArray() to freeze the results at a specific point in time.

data.title: Exercise: Student Grade Analyzer
data.description: Use LINQ to analyze a list of student grades and produce a summary report.
steps: Create a Student class with Name, Subject, and Score properties.
Create a list of at least 10 students across 3 subjects.
Use LINQ to find the student with the highest score in each subject.
Calculate the average score per subject using GroupBy and Average.
List all students who scored below 60 (failing) using Where.
Rank the top 3 students overall by total score using OrderByDescending and Take.
data.expectedOutcome: A console program that prints per-subject toppers, averages, failing students, and the top 3 overall scorers — all using LINQ operators.

items.question: Does LINQ only work with in-memory collections?
items.answer: No — LINQ to Objects works with in-memory collections. LINQ to SQL, LINQ to Entities (Entity Framework), and LINQ to XML work with databases and XML files. All share the same operator names but are implemented differently.

items.question: Is LINQ slower than a hand-written foreach loop?
items.answer: LINQ has a small overhead from lambda invocation and iterator allocation. For most business-logic scenarios the difference is negligible. Profile before optimizing — LINQ's readability usually outweighs the micro-optimization.

items.question: What does deferred execution mean in practice?
items.answer: The query is not evaluated until you loop over it or call a terminal operator like ToList(). This means if the source changes after query construction, results may change. Use ToList() to capture a snapshot.

items.question: Can I use LINQ on arrays?
items.answer: Yes — arrays implement IEnumerable<T>, so all LINQ operators work directly on them. No conversion needed.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: LINQ provides a unified query experience across collections, databases, and XML
Method syntax and query syntax are equivalent — choose based on readability
Common operators: Where, Select, OrderBy, GroupBy, Join, Count, Sum
Deferred execution means queries run when iterated, not when defined
Call ToList() to force immediate execution and freeze results
LINQ replaces verbose loops with expressive, composable chains
data.takeaway: LINQ is one of the most productive features in C#. Once comfortable with it, you will reach for it in almost every data-manipulation task.
